p:
I really appreciate your question and uhm, and thank you for the kind of

continued advocacy. It is true, so typically when we uh, particularly if we’re talking about a safety surface and that sort of piece where you see a safety surface starting to buckle. We typically like to see instead of doing this kind of targeted repair, we want to see uh and want to deliver for the community. If this is going to be our time when we have a shutdown of this playground, we want to deliver as much new kind of improvements to this space as possible. We definitely don't want to do a piecemeal approach where we have to close it down for safety surface but then we don’t use the opportunity to create more ADA accessibility or we don’t use the opportunity to frankly redesign the space so that it’s more age appropriate, where we have 3 to 5 area space and then a larger, kind of big kid space and then maybe expand it to swingsets and those kinds of pieces. It does mean bigger scope and bigger projects. Uhm, but typically it’s been our kind of policy to try to - to try to do as much good in one go as possible but I hear your question too about then having to wait years for something that starts out as simple as safety surface.

So, what I’d say is that in the Bronx, we actually have seen some success with maybe trying to have our cake and eat it too essentially, where we do kind of focus on raising the funds, getting together a big capital project but not letting that be the reason why your constituents don’t see any sort of improvement between that and you know five years from now whenever it happens. So, what we can do in house where we can think through creatively to show a little bit more investment, I really call that low hanging fruit and I think we need to double down and do more of that. So, what I’d say is that you know it is - we are interested in trying to just be in there once, do one disruption, do as much good as possible and get out of there. It shouldn’t be uhm, an excuse for your constituents not to see any sort of increased attention to a space. So, we’re happy to work with you. Jessie Aponte as you mentioned, is a great Borough Commissioner who kind of focuses on this too but in my capacity as possible, we should - we should work together to try to find other opportunities to show at least a little bit of increased care for these spaces that are very important.

Yeah, thank you so much Commissioner. I appreciate that and I appreciate the partnership. I just like double want to emphasize format. I got a big problem. I heard there was like a contractor issue. Get our money back. Please replace those floor mats on the new ones that are still rising up. Just a side bar. Uhm, second question - oh wow, okay. Second question and then I’ll just bundle in the third one. Uhm, how is it possible that $50 million is enough to renovate or reconstruct 10 parks through the Community Parks initiative? Because every, almost every estimate that I have for an upgrade in District 14 is like $11 million, $20 million, $50 million. That’s question 2. Question 3 is around Bailey Playground and the example of that being a park across the street from a big housing, next to the highway, like certainly in an environmental justice highlighted park that hasn’t seen an upgrade I want to say in decades. Uhm, I can’t quite figure it out. Just want to understand how a park like Bailey Playground can be in the new need priority category for parks for years and years and years but not see upgrades and then the last question, sorry, thank you

Chair. Thank you Chair. So, that’s question 2 and then the 3rd question is just any updates on swim education. Uh, as a dominican who can’t swim, I am particularly interested in what the Parks Department is doing with the laws that the previous Council passed.

Yes, thank you so much. I really appreciate your question about CPI. It’s just my favorite. I’m allowed to have favorites. It’s my favorite funding initiative. Uhm, so just very broadly, the City Parks Initiative which we just very proudly announced, our kind of new parks that we’re going to be undertaking major renovations on is uh, one of our premier kind of equity driven capital initiative- uh programs where we’re typically as you know, a lot of the funding priorities that come to us, the capital projects come from Council Members taking it on with advocacy groups or a Borough President may be taking it on with an advocacy group but it can just be based on maybe popularity or like kind of where you’re hearing the most voices, but that can often can lead to a little bit of an inequity around the parks that are also serving

populations of people but are not getting the investment that they need. So, that’s when uh several years ago, we decided to try a new approach that was based on parks that have not been renovated in like 20 years plus, that were also serving vulnerable, underserved, underinvested in communities and what we could do with a pot of money that could really inject some major capital improvements there. I will tell you that you’re right, that the $50 million is kind of like a starting number but it actually is not encompassing all of what’s happening and your investments, even if they are $1 million, $50,000 or $500,000, $300,000, that actually take - we take that into account when we look at which projects we’re going to fund next for CPI because it shows that there is a Council Member, a Borough President, somebody who has got some skin in the game who like, who knows that this is a renovation that’s really worth it. I’m going to give you one example from Manhattan, because I know this best but Council Member Salaam funded St. Nicholas Park for $2 million just maybe a year ago. St. Nicholas Park is a massive park and it

was supposed to be just for a little tiny playground. Then Borough President Mark Levine funded that project another $1 million. So, technically, it could have been done right there with the $3 million. But then we saw that there was an opportunity with CPI that this whole area had not been invested in for over 20 years, 25 years. So, we decided to put additional CPI funding into that project and then we uhm, to kind of increase the overall scope of that project, start dealing with erosion issues, start dealing with the adjacent basketball courts, barbeque areas, picnic tables, and on top of that, we were able to tap into some baseline funding for public restroom buildings. So, now, all of a sudden a project that started with Council Member Salaam’s $2 million, that could be your $1 million, has now ballooned to $14 million that could actually deliver big changes for that one park in that one area. So, I’d say thank you for asking about it. It is a tremendous initiative. Something that I’m very proud of. Something that I think we should be doing more of. Data driven equity lens sort of work that looks at capital projects and what can happen with it

uhm and what I’d say is that we’ll happily look at Bailey Playground. We’ll happily keep this in mind. We want to work with you on thinking through additional projects and where they’re needed but please don’t forget to fund them, even with modest amounts of money because that does make an impact on us and how we think about kind of prioritizing projects. And then when it comes to swim education, we are very proud of what we’re doing. I’m happy to give you more numbers on this. I don’t know how much time we have but if we are able to provide a little more time here, I’d tell you that we are increasingly partnering with New York City Public Schools, with other partners like Asphalt Green and others and then doing our own swim education to try to serve and teach the kids how to swim, as many as possible. I think that in kind of this concerted effort has been undergoing for just a couple years and we’re just hitting, I think hopefully aiming for around 5,000 young people to learn how to swim in this next year. Although I’ll look to our Deputy Commissioner Margaret Nelson to confirm that number for me. Uhm,

there is always more to do. That $5,000 is not every single second grader. We would love to have more. Even though you’re not in second grade, I want you to know how to swim and others. So, you know we’re constantly in conversation. I was just in the conversation with your Borough President, uh about, thinking about access to water, access to pools and trying to see, think through creative ways, partnering with the YMCA, partnering with others, looking at pools that are defunct, even if they’re not parks to think through how do we kind of comprehensively think about access to water and access to swim plazas.
Thank you Chair for the time. Matt Drury is the best by the way. Good to see you.
Yes, he is.
Alright, uhm, we’re going to go to Southern Brooklyn, Council Member Susan Zhuang and following some questions from your neighbor Council Member Kayla Santosuosso.
Thank you. Very nice to see you in person, Commissioner.
Nice to see you too.
We’re excited. After the meeting, you actually comfort my team uh, and we see the hope for Southern Brooklyn.
Thank you.

And then we have, I have some questions. First in my district, we have a lot of huge trees. During the storm, it’s always damaged the house roof and sometimes in the storm, fell down and have the branch dropped on the cars, break the car windshields. We haven't seen any improvement in this type of situation?

Mmm, mmm, thank you for the question and it’s good to see you in person too. I’m really looking forward to working with you and your team. You know, during storms when it comes to tree damage, it’s you would think that it’s these bigger trees are the only ones that are susceptible to storms, but the truth is, is that any type of tree, be it a small new tree or a large hopefully not but often times like 40, 50, 60 year old tree can also be down in a storm and truthfully as with - we were just talking about this infrastructure, trees are very important. This is living infrastructure. It is common to see this butt up with other types of

infrastructure like our streets where folks are parked. I believe that when it comes to kind of claims on this, any sort of claim for damage should be directed to the comptroller's office to issue those claims. I’m happy to work with you and your office to make sure that constituents understand this. The best uh but really the best kind of uh approach and offense to this type of damage is regular block pruning. That’s the best thing that we do, meaning that like on a 7 year basis, all of the trees in your neighborhood need to be pruned. And that means that we go through proactively before a storm hits, cutting down extra branches, making sure that there’s no interruption with the other kind of powerlines or things like that and that’s the - that’s the kind of goal of the Parks Department is to make sure that every block in every neighborhood is pruned on a 7 year basis.

Thank you and I’m going to - my team is going to follow up with you because it’s always the same block every single year, have the same issue and we have been sending out emails and letters to the previous Commissioner. We did not get a response.
I’d be more than happy to make sure to look into this so please do. We’re happy to follow up with you.

Thank you. And also my colleagues talk about the dog waste. I actually have a good idea for you. We need more PEP Officers. They can help to address this issue. And also they can help to generate the revenue for the city. I just want to know how many PEP Officers you have right now? How many you think you need? And I rarely see any PEP Officer in my neighborhood and I believe, personally believe they are peace makers because they don’t carry any weapon but they come to talk to the people in the community and they make sure everything goes smooth and the people, well and the kids actually see them. The bad behavior they have in the park actually, they behave themselves better.

Thank you. Thank you, thank you for your support of PEP. We appreciate it. We appreciate you talking about them being peace keepers. They are certified peace keepers. They do provide I believe a holistic sense of safety. It’s eyes in the park. It’s education. They are

incredibly important. To specifically answer your question, we have 254 PEP Officers who are baselined plus 100 through this one shot funding, which we’ve discussed today. So, that’s 300, currently 300. We are funded for 354 PEP Officers. And in terms of how many we’d like, again, I would welcome as many - more is more in this case and I of course would welcome any number of additional resources, as kind of the leader of this agency and thinking through our resources. What we do with what we have is to make sure that we’re using a data driven approach to deploying our PEP Officers, making sure that we’re going to where the people are. Now you actually have this data too and I’m happy to follow up with your team to make sure that we’re following up because we just launched the vital parks explorer, just in the last few years where you can actually go based on Council District or by community board district and look at how frequently PEP is in your parks. So, we’re happy to look at this with you to make sure that your constituents understand how frequently they are there but I also hear you that ultimately,

even if we have our PEP’s Officers who are making visits there, it’s a sense of safety and you want to have eyes in the park. You’d like to see - we do understand that PEP Officers do provide this kind of sense of uniformed presence in the park and we very much appreciate your kind of ongoing advocacy there.
But if we - if the park hire additional 200 PEP Officers, how much is it going to cost for the city?
Oh, well, I think 100- the one shot funding that was allocated to us last year, uh, was for 100 PEP Officers. And so, it’s $20 million for 200 officers, I think is the -
So, is that same amount going to happen this year or?

You know, ultimately the one shots are the product of the conversations between the Council and the Administration during the budget process. We really appreciate the advocacy that this Council, you and your colleagues have done in the past and we’re, you know, happy to continue to do this work with whatever resources that we’re given.
Okay, thank you.
Yeah, thank you.
Okay, so we have been going for about 3 hours. Commissioner, would you like to take a 5 minute break?
I could do this all day. Let’s keep on going.
I want to be courteous. I want to be courteous.
You’re very sweet.

Okay. Given that we’re going to jump online, uhm, we’re going to instead of Southern Brooklyn, we’re going to go to Brownsville Brooklyn and then Southern Brooklyn. So, we’re going to jump to Council Member Darlene Mealy, who has been online and then Council Member Virginia Maloney. Council Member, I think you have to unmute.
Good afternoon.
Good afternoon. There we go.

Thank you. I was just wanted - congratulations to our new Commissioner. I have not met you as of yet but I would love to know uhm, I had a quick question. We have - I was in office, came out of office, and now I’m back in office and I gave money for a comfort station at

Lincoln Terrace Park and I was wondering, could you tell me uhm, what’s the status of that and what is the hold up? The community - I mean, I go there a lot and it’s sad how they say, when is this going to be finished? You know Eastern Park - Buffalo Avenue is almost like an 8 lane highway. So, for that comfort station to be there, that would be a tremendous help to this city and to my community. So, could you please give me uh, uhm, at least a status on this comfort station? Thank you Chair for giving me this opportunity.

Hi Council Member. Thank you so much for your question. It’s really lovely to meet you and I’m looking forward to meeting you in your district in person. I would absolutely be happy to walk through with you in any park, if it’s Lincoln Terrace Park or any other one. I’m looking forward to working with you and thank you so much for your question about funding. So, I do not have at my fingertips here a current status, however, there are two pieces. One, I’ll be sure to get back to you directly with where we stand but you can also look online. We have what’s called a capital tracker as part of our Parks website. You

can just google capital tracker and typically for any capital project that we have fully funded in our queue. We have - I put together this kind of data tool online where you can look up exactly where a project is, if it’s in design, procurement, if it’s in construction, anticipated timeline. I - you know, certainly, I don’t want to have to have any of your constituents go through a website to try to learn this but we are trying to just make sure that more information about timeline is available.

Commissioner, I don’t know if you understand the severity of this. I gave about $2.5 million or $3 million for this comfort station. That was almost 18 years ago. If I did not get back in office, I don’t know where that money would have went. When the community graced me with another opportunity to serve then, the first thing was why we do not have this comfort station. So, the Department of Parks had the money, did not do what they said they was going to do with the money and now that I’m back in office, it’s been 4 years and the first year I came in, I said, where is my comfort station and they started working on it. Now it’s 4 years and still nothing. So, it’s not

about looking it up, it’s about seeing what is the hold up and why you have the city money and we cannot have a comfort station. And it needs to have some kind of budgetary timeline on it because the community deserves it. And if the Chair could give me another opportunity to ask one more question, I would love to but I would love to get authorization first.
Sure, absolutely, yes ma’am.

Thank you uhm, I definitely need that question and we talk about preservation, uhm, uh, horticulture in Lincoln Terrace Park, I’ve done 2 press conferences inside the parks. I did 1 in Harlem, 1 in Brooklyn. Could you tell me - are your horticulture or your people are still using Round Tree to clean our public parks?
Council Member, are you referring to Roundup?
Oh, Roundup, I’m sorry. Yes, Roundup.

Not a problem. I can confirm that our - so uh, a person with local law, Parks

Department isn’t generally able to use synthetic pesticides, which would include like phosphate.

That passed and I came back like 20 uh, 23 and you were still using it. I had a meeting with you and you were still using Roundup. So, I ask that you really look into that and stop using that for this whole city. New York cannot handle that and remember, our young people are going into these parks. Our dogs are eating some of the grass and that’s a detriment to their health. So, do you want to have a conversation later in regards to that?

Absolutely. You know we’re happy - I will happily look into this more. I definitely understand the stakes here. I too have a 3 and a 6 year old who are in the parks, in our planting beds far too often, even when they’re not supposed to be so we understand the importance of this. This is frankly why we have very, kind of what I think is crazy ways of killing rats and things like that because we are very careful about what type of poisons and pesticides and things like that, that we’re using in our parks. So, we will happily get

back to you and confirm what’s being used and what’s not being used.

I thank you for that and you can check uhm, the Black institute. I did two press conferences and we keep looking into it and it’s still - you’re still using it. So, please could you talk to me. The environment deserves better. Thank you so much Chair.
Not a problem. Alright, I want to acknowledge Council Members Alexa Avilés, and Lincoln Restler who we’ve been joined by. At this time, we’re going to go to Council Member Virginia Maloney.

Thank you very much Chair and thank you Commissioner Shimamura. It’s great to see you here and as a Manhattanite, congratulations on your role. I have to ask about District 4 Parks, which is one of the lowest ratios of parkland per resident in the city and my office has received a lot of inquiries regarding the ongoing closure and renovation of the Tutor City Playground and uhm, that’s located on 42nd Street. I’m wondering if you could give me a clear update on the timeline for when it plans to reopen and the cause

for delays if any and what steps you’re taking to improve communication with the community on this project.

Yeah, thank you so much Council Member for the question. So, we’ll have to get back to you specifically about where we stand with the Tutor City Playground project but I am somewhat familiar with both this playground and the playground that’s across the street. You have 2 kind of sister playgrounds, one on each side and I will say that I will recall from my time as Borough Commissioner that in understanding when and the timeline for Tutor City’s Playground reconstruction, we really were thinking through, also making sure that your community has also access to the one across the street. It does not replace it by any means but like how we think about any time there is scaffolding in a park, anytime a playground has to get closed down. We take this really seriously and particularly when we’re going into the spring and summer months, it’s not something that we do lightly. So, where we can either allow for partial access, where we can try to push this work to be only relegated to some portion or phasing of projects.

That’s really going to be our approach whenever possible. We’ll get back to you specifically about where we stand with Tutor City Playground but overall just know that we understand the significance of access particularly in your district but really across the city and wherever we can, we’re going to limit that.

Thank you for that update and we will be following up. I also wanted to ask about park concessions revenue, which the preliminary budget shows has dropped by nearly $9 million. I’m wondering if you can give more information on the breakdown of the cause, specific concession sites or contracts or any specific locations that account for those losses and uh also what steps the agency is taking to backfill lost concession revenue?

Yeah, thank you for your question. I really appreciate the attention to the role that Parks plays. It may not be as much as our agencies but we’re really proud of our contributions to the overall fiscal health of our city and ways that we bring in revenue, particularly and I’ll flag our Assistant Commissioner of -I’m sorry, I forget

the actual title that you have. But uhm, who is also here to uh - who can answer a little bit more on this but overall, you know I’m not sure where the $9 million kind of uh, oh, oh yeah, I’m not sure where I see it like uh going down in kind of overall budget here but we do contribute over $50 million per year to the general fund in terms of our concessions and other kind of opportunities that we bring to parks. I mentioned this earlier but you know we find in general that the type of concessions that we bring in. The type of businesses that we work with, really does provide a benefit to our parks. So, people like to have access to sandwiches and drinks and food options. They like to take advantage of opportunities either to rent a bike and go bike riding through the park or in the case of Central Park to rent a sailboat and sail through the sailboat piece. There’s also, it’s also an opportunity for us because we don’t have necessarily a kind of strict targets to meet or high, extremely high targets to meet. It gives us an opportunity to be creative with our type of concessions that we look out for and a good example is what you’ll see in City Hall Park.

In just a couple weeks from now, we partnered with the Workers Justice Project, those deliveristas to create, to take over one of our what was a news stand and then turn it into a bike, battery kind of library system, where you can swap out those batteries, get some tuning of your bike done. It is also a concession of ours and we’re really excited about how that’s going to compliment and provide essential services to New Yorkers. So, it’s a really diverse portfolio. I’ll look to our Assistant Commissioner to see if there’s anything else he wants to add about this portfolio of revenue concessions. Forgive me David forgetting your exact title but uhm, we’re really excited about kind of the opportunities ahead and I’d say the last piece is that we’re deeply committed to making sure that the type of opportunities that we have to do business with parks and to do business with the city are diverse and accessible to as many people as possible.

Please raise your right hand. Thank you. Uh, do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth in your

testimony before this Committee and to respond honestly to Council Member questions.

Yes. Hi Council Member. Thank you for the question. I’m David Cerron, Assistant Commissioner for Business Development special events. Apologies for any confusion, you know the good news is, we are doing well this year. We’re tracking ahead of the same time last year. Our revenue target for OMB for this fiscal year is $54 million. We do intend to meet that goal. As the Commissioner mentioned, you know we are always seeking to do more, looking for creative ways to make our parks engaging and fun and activate our open spaces. So, you know if you have ideas, if there’s other suggestions that you’d like us to look into, we’d be thrilled.
Thank you very much and thank you Chair.
Okay, uh, we are going to go over to is that Western Brooklyn? Yeah, okay, Council Member Lincoln Restler.

Thank you so much Chair, appreciate your thoughtful leadership of this Committee and Commissioner, it’s great to see you. I

want to thank you for being so generous with your time earlier this month or last month in meeting with me and my team and talking through I don’t know 100 parks related issues in District 33. We could have gone on for hours but uhm, you were incredibly gracious and really appreciate your thoughtfulness and eagerness to partner, which really comes through in every appearance you have before the Council and in every conversation I have had with you. Uhm, I apologize that I’m late, so I may be bothering you about something that’s already come up but as I think you heard me say before, I’ve been deeply concerned about the reduction in part time headcount in the Parks Department. You know in the Adams Administration, we lost 1,600 part time workers. It’s had an enormous impact on the conditions in our park and so, while the full time headcount has been steady, the reduction in the part time headcount uh, has been a major concern for me and for members of my community as they look around their parks every day. Could you give some insight into what you’re planning for currently for headcount, for the part time headcount for next year and uh, how we can be

helpful in supporting your efforts to ensure that parks is fully staffed?

Yeah, thank you so much Council Member, it’s really lovely to work with you always. Uhm, and I really appreciate the focus here. So, in the short term and speaking of part time headcount, uhm I think through also what our seasonal headcount it going to be. We in general and we actually haven't covered this yet. In general, we jump from a 5,000 person agency to nearly 10,000 for our summer season and that includes all types of roles but the vast majority of those come in the form of maintenance and operation staff. On top of that, we also do lifeguards this way, summer camp programs this way, additional kind of recreational folks that come on board. Everything else in between but really that’s - we double frankly in size. You know for the next - for this budget cycle, what we see is essentially uhm, the differences those one shot funding items is where uhm, is where you see that big differential between - it’s essentially what would be the budget that was given to us in the last fiscal year that those one shot items reflect, 277

positions and they crawl across the spectrum from Green Thumb Park Rangers, PEP Officers, maintenance folks and others. Uhm, so certainly, as was mentioned before, they are highly supplemental uhm, to these units. The Chair has recognized that PEP is essentially, the one shots essentially reflect one-third of our entire workforce there for something like rangers. I think it’s almost 50 percent of that workforce. And so, we very much greatly appreciate the kind of one shot funding here and it is a major part of our overall operations.

You know when we - for the analysis that’s shared with us, when we look at the FY22 headcount for part time workers, which I think includes the seasonal workforce. It was counted at 44,060 workers. As of FY26, our current fiscal year, it was down to 27,074. So, a major 1,600 plus person reduction and you know, I think that there are lots of different ways that parks can count this and look at this and to be fair, we saw a meaningful increase in the full time headcount during that same period. But the significant reduction in the part time headcount

is something that I’m really hoping we can fix together in this budget. So, you know prelim is the beginning of this conversation. We’ve got 3 more months to go. I’m certainly eager to support the Chairs efforts to help us increase headcount at the Parks Department. I think it’s one of the areas that we frankly just over the last 3 years got an enormous amount of pushback from Mayor Adams and his budget team and we shouldn’t have. And I’m hopeful that if the Council is willing to put up the resources and we’re willing to fight for the Parks Department that we’ll have a much more cooperative partner on the other side of City Hall. I know we do in our Parks Commissioner. Uhm, I heard some of my colleagues ask and Council Member Zhuang in particular about pruning and tree management. I’ll just add, I know that this was a tough winter and a tough storm and I know that there were some declines in the first few months of this year as a result of a contractor passing away. You know the CEO of a contractor passing away but the timelines on pruning, the reductions in total pruning, the timelines I’m getting, hanging tree limbs removed

from the most urgent cases to the least urgent cases. I think all of the timelines are really unacceptable so I really hope that this is something that you can look at with the team and help to speed up. I just wanted to highlight a couple other items in my last 19 seconds. One is, I’m just you know, MET pool has been a real source of frustration. Members of my community are having a protest this Wednesday uhm about the conditions and the fact that it’s been closed so long. We had tried to get the Parks Department to begin the capital project while they were trying to identify interim repairs. I don’t think that happened and so, we’re looking at an extended closure there. Uhm, would love to get an update on Parks containerization of garbage. I know there was funding in last year's budget for that. My office has funded parks containerization of garbage at Cadman Plaza, WNYC Transmitter, McCarren, McGolrick, and other parks, which my community is thrilled about. I think you guys are putting in the money, so I don’t need to cover anymore, which is great but would love real updates on that.

And then lastly, and then I’ll let you talk, is uhm, thrilled with their - well, briefly on two things. Thrilled that Deputy Commissioner Boorstyn and others have been really helpful in supporting the Karen Asphalt project, $15 million parks project in Williamsburgh that we’re thrilled about, really appreciative of parks partnership there. And then lastly, Anchorage Plaza in Dumbo. We just heard from David, you have a terrific lead on your concessions team and really appreciate all of his partnership. We’re trying to figure out if there’s some compromise between vendors and the pickleball vendor. You know the street vendors and the pickleball vendor to share that space. I know that you’re looking into it. Is that something that we can follow up on as well?
Sure.
I’m sorry for peppering you with so many questions.

No, it’s great and thank you. I’m going to look for our Acting First Deputy Commissioner to come up just to talk about the containerization piece but I think that I can handle these other ones.

So, I think we owe you a follow up conversation around Anchorage Plaza. It is tough because ultimately even in the case where if we were to kind of rethink this space, we still need to have kind of parks appropriate uses on these spaces and when it comes to vending and that sort of thing it just gets tough but happy to follow up with you on that. I know it’s important to you.
Thank you.

When it comes to pruning, yes, you - I mean, you clearly you have read our PMMR and like know that this is in part due to our contracting piece. What I’ll tell you is that there’s a bigger understanding that relying on the contractors that we have, relying on this pool is the wrong - is the wrong method.
Here, here.

We need to diversify. We need to think it through. We need to continue to pilot things like in house planting, in house pruning, but we need to diversify the size and scope of our contracts. We want to keep cost down but also to get this work done faster and to make sure that we’re not building an environment in an atmosphere out there

that’s not sustainable and just dangerous in so many ways. So, we definitely hear you on that. This is a frustrating piece to be in but we’re on the right track. I plan on coming back to you in many future hearings with better numbers on pruning but ultimately, there’s a bigger push here to make sure that we are consciously thinking about how we do contracting to build in uhm, to build in different size scope and add more diversity to this whole pool. Uh, format pool, speaking of pools. In my first 6 weeks on this job, MET pool was a priority visit from mine. So, I can tell you that I, myself, have visited this site because I know how deeply important it is to the community. I too have heard them. I understand the rallies.
